title: FedSSA: Aligning Graphs Across Federated Sites
one_liner: When a graph lives in pieces on different computers, the paper learns what each piece looks like and nudges them toward a shared middle ground so they can learn together.
lead: Imagine each hospital has its own patient network: doctors are nodes, connections are referrals. Hospital A's network looks very different from Hospital B's — different node types, different connection patterns. Federated learning means each hospital keeps its data private and sends only model updates to a central server. The problem: when each hospital's graph is so different, the model trained at the center is useful to nobody. This paper proposes a method that first understands what makes each hospital unique, groups hospitals with similar patterns, and steers each hospital's model toward its group's average so they can all learn together.

problem.h2: Why federated learning on graphs breaks when sites differ
paras: When a graph is split across multiple sites (hospitals, companies, countries), each site keeps its own edges and node features private. They send only model updates to a central server, never the raw data. This is federated learning, and it protects privacy.

The trouble: each site's graph is different. Hospital A's doctors connect by specialty; Hospital B's connect by geographic region. One uses doctor IDs as node features; the other uses patient counts. When the central server averages model updates from such different graphs, the shared model fits nobody. A naive approach treats all sites as identical and averages their weights directly — but this pulls the model in conflicting directions.
The core issue: the server cannot see each site's graph or features, so it has no idea which sites should be trusted together and which are too different.

callout.html: The paper infers what each site's graph looks like, clusters similar sites, and steers each site toward its cluster's middle ground instead of blindly averaging.

steps.text: Each site trains a small statistical model to estimate what kinds of nodes it has and how often without sharing raw data.
The server groups sites by how similar their node mixes are, using a clustering algorithm.
For each cluster, the server averages the model updates from only sites in that cluster.
The server uses spectral methods to measure each site's graph topology and steers spectral properties toward its cluster's average.
Each site receives updates that pull it toward its cluster, not the global center.

paras: Instead of averaging model weights from all sites equally, the method first learns which sites are similar and then averages only within similarity groups. The model is steered toward its group's center, not the global center.

hidden.name: Semantic drift
paras: When a site trains its model on its own local graph, the model's learned weights drift away from what a generic graph-model would learn. This drift reflects the site's unique features and structure. The paper calls this drift the signature of each site.

The method estimates this drift by running a variational inference model at each site — essentially a small statistical encoder that learns to reproduce each site's node mix without sending the raw nodes to the server. The server uses this sketch to figure out which sites have similar node types and which are different.

heat.caption: Darker means the site's node mix or graph structure is more different from the global average. Highlighted cells are measured by the method.

reads.html: A site's signature is how lopsided its nodes are — what fraction are doctors versus nurses, for example.
The method infers a variational distribution (a probabilistic model) of the node-feature histogram at each site and uses the numbers learned by that model as a compact summary.

paras: First, the method lets each site estimate its own node-distribution signature using variational inference. This is a small, private calculation at each site that produces a sketch of the site's node mix without ever sending the raw nodes. The server receives only this sketch.

Second, the server clusters the sketches. Sites with similar sketches are grouped. Importantly, the method also measures graph structure using spectral methods (a mathematical way to characterize how connected the graph is and in what patterns). Sites with similar spectral properties cluster together.

Third, instead of averaging all model updates to a global center, each site is pulled toward the center of its cluster. This works because sites in the same cluster are similar enough that a shared model makes sense for them. The spectral measure ensures that graph topology also gets aligned, not just node features.

Why does this work? Because sites with similar graphs benefit from the same model, while trying to use a single global model for very different graphs just confuses each one. By partitioning sites by similarity and aligning within groups, the method gives each group a model that actually fits them. Each group learns faster because every site is pulling in a compatible direction.

math.words: Each site's loss is the local training loss plus a penalty that pulls the site's model toward its cluster average. The penalty is weighted by how different the site is from its cluster.
math.equation: L_site = L_train + lambda * distance(model_site, model_cluster) + mu * spectral_distance

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose Site A trains and gets loss 0.5. Its cluster average model is 10% different in weight values.
Spectral distance = 0.05 (the graphs are mostly similar). mu = 1.0. Spectral penalty = 1.0 * 0.05 = 0.05.
Total loss = 0.5 + 0.2 + 0.05 = 0.75. The model is pulled toward its cluster, not the global center.

math.note: The equation ensures that each site learns well locally and stays close to sites like itself.

charts.title: Naive average (all sites)
charts.note: Blindly averaging pulls both sites toward a middle ground that neither likes.

charts.title: FedSSA (aligned clusters)
charts.note: Each site is pulled toward its cluster center instead of the global center, so both improve because now the target model actually matches their graphs.

items.b: Sites with completely disjoint node types.
items.html: If Site A has only doctor nodes and Site B has only patient nodes, no clustering will find them similar. The method assumes sites share some node types so that a statistical sketch can reveal what they have in common.

If one site's graph is a star (one central hub) and another is a ring (everyone equally connected), spectral energy measures will diverge sharply. Alignment cannot fix this because the underlying graph structures are fundamentally different — no model can simultaneously optimize for a hub-and-spoke network and a full peer-to-peer network.

If a cluster has only one or two sites, the cluster center is unreliable and might overfit to those few sites. The method works best when each cluster has at least five or more sites with similar patterns so the center represents a stable trend.

When sites have enough feature overlap and graph structures are reasonably similar, the method discovers the true clusters and steers each site toward a representative that actually matches its graph.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a toy federated learning setup with five simulated sites. Each site has a graph with 20 nodes. Sites A, B, C have similar node-feature distributions; Sites D, E are different. Without alignment, train all sites naively. With alignment, use FedSSA to cluster and align. Measure the accuracy of each site after five rounds of federated training.
demo.closing: The demo should show that aligned sites (A, B, C) stay close to each other in accuracy and drift less from their starting performance, while naive averaging pulls all sites toward an unhelpful center.
